prompt: The planner calls the camera API, and `Info.plist` has no `NSCameraUsageDescription`. What happens?
hint: Section 02 quotes Apple's documentation on that key.

choices.text: iOS shows the alert with a default sentence
choices.why: There is no default sentence: the key is required, and its absence stops the app.

choices.text: iOS stops the app when it asks
choices.why: Right. And no build step warned about it, which is why section 06 checks the file.

choices.text: The camera opens, and the alert is skipped for that one session
choices.why: Nothing reaches the camera without the person's answer, and that answer needs the string.

choices.text: Xcode refuses to build the app until the key is added
choices.why: The build succeeds; the failure arrives at the first tap on the camera button.

prompt: Which usage string does guideline 5.1.1 ask for?
hint: A reason, in terms of something the person wants.

choices.text: "Planner needs access to your camera."
choices.why: That states a need and no use; the guideline asks the string to describe the use.

choices.text: "Allow camera access to continue using Planner."
choices.why: It describes nothing, and it pressures: 5.1.1(iv) forbids forcing consent.

choices.text: "Planner uses the camera to photograph your notes for a session."
choices.why: Right: it says what the access is for, clearly and completely.

choices.text: "NSCameraUsageDescription"
choices.why: That is the key's name; the person would see it as the reason.

prompt: A person tapped *Don't Allow* yesterday. Today the app calls the request method again. What does the person see?
hint: The system stores the answer.

choices.text: Nothing: the call returns the stored answer
choices.why: Right. The alert is shown once, and after that only Settings can change the answer.

choices.text: The same alert, because every call asks
choices.why: The system asks once and stores the status.

choices.text: A different alert asking them to reconsider
choices.why: iOS has no second alert; that is why section 07 exists.

choices.text: The Settings app, opened automatically by iOS
choices.why: Only the app can offer to open Settings, and only when the person taps a button.

prompt: Match each kind of access to the key `Info.plist` needs.
hint: The table in section 02.

prompt: Which camera state is the only one where `requestAccess` shows the alert?
hint: Nobody has answered yet.

choices.text: `.denied`
choices.why: A denied state is the answer already given; the call returns it.

choices.text: `.restricted` by Screen Time
choices.why: Somebody else set it, and the person cannot change it either.

choices.text: `.notDetermined`
choices.why: Right: nobody has asked yet, so iOS asks now.

choices.text: `.authorized`
choices.why: The person already said yes.

prompt: Why does attaching an existing photo with `PhotosPicker` need no usage string?
hint: Where does the picker run?

choices.text: Photos are less private than the camera, so iOS treats them as public data
choices.why: A library can be more private than the camera; the reason is who sees it.

choices.text: The picker runs outside the app, which sees only the photo chosen
choices.why: Right. The app is never given the library, so there is nothing to ask for.

choices.text: SwiftUI asks on the app's behalf with its own sentence
choices.why: No alert appears at all for the out-of-process picker.

choices.text: The usage string is only checked by App Review, not by iOS
choices.why: iOS checks it too: the camera call without its key stops the app.

prompt: `cameraAllowed()` ends its `switch` with `@unknown default: return false`. Why is that case there?
hint: The enumeration belongs to Apple.

choices.text: To catch an error thrown by `requestAccess`
choices.why: `requestAccess` does not throw; it returns a Bool.

choices.text: Because `.restricted` is not a real case
choices.why: It is real, and it is handled on the line above.

choices.text: A future enum case needs an answer now
choices.why: Right, and here an unknown state means no camera.

choices.text: Swift needs it for every switch over an enum
choices.why: A switch over your own enum needs none; section 07's has no default at all.

prompt: A school manages its students' iPhones and has switched the camera off. Which state does the planner see, and what should its button offer?
hint: Who made the decision, and can the student undo it?

choices.text: `.denied`, with a button to open Settings
choices.why: The student did not deny anything, and the switch in Settings is not theirs to turn.

choices.text: `.restricted`, with a sentence and no Settings button
choices.why: Right: somebody else decided, so sending them to Settings would be a dead end.

choices.text: `.notDetermined`, so the app can ask the student
choices.why: Asking is pointless when the device's manager has already decided.

choices.text: `.authorized`, since the school granted the app
choices.why: Turning the camera off is the opposite of granting it.

prompt: Which location level does Apple's article call the preferred choice?
hint: Better privacy and better battery life.

choices.text: Always, so updates arrive in the background
choices.why: Always is for when it is necessary; the article prefers the other.

choices.text: When In Use
choices.why: Right, in the article's words: better privacy and battery life implications.

choices.text: Neither: precise location is the preferred choice
choices.why: Precision is a separate setting; the article compares the two levels.

choices.text: Whichever the person picks in the alert
choices.why: The app chooses which level to ask for; the article says which to prefer.

prompt: Why does the planner ask for no location at all?
hint: Compare the feature with the permission it would need.

choices.text: Location does not work on an iPhone without a GPS chip or a SIM card
choices.why: Every iPhone can locate itself; the question is whether the planner should.

choices.text: App Review rejects every study app that uses location
choices.why: The guideline asks for relevance to the core function, not a ban by category.

choices.text: The only use proposed needs Always, and a timed reminder solves it
choices.why: Right: a stronger permission than the problem needs has not earned its place.

choices.text: Core Location is not available to SwiftUI apps
choices.why: Any iOS app can use Core Location; section 04 shows the code.

prompt: `requestWhenInUseAuthorization()` returns at once; the person's answer arrives later in the location manager's ___.
hint: The object that `manager.delegate = self` names.

prompt: Which of these is tracking, in Apple's sense, and needs App Tracking Transparency?
hint: Linking with other companies' data, for advertising.

choices.text: Saving the plan on the planner's own server, for backup
choices.why: Keeping your own users' data for your own app is not tracking.

choices.text: Counting crashes to fix the app
choices.why: That is diagnostics for your own app, not linking with others' data.

choices.text: Sending an ad network an ID to match across apps
choices.why: Right: that links your data with other companies' for advertising.

choices.text: Remembering the last open course in `UserDefaults`
choices.why: That is a required-reason API, declared in the manifest, not tracking.

prompt: What does the documentation for `NSUserTrackingUsageDescription` say happens without the key?
hint: Section 05 quotes it.

choices.text: The app crashes when it uses the framework
choices.why: Right, the same failure as the camera without its key.

choices.text: The alert shows a generic sentence about advertising
choices.why: There is no generic sentence; the key is required.

choices.text: Tracking is allowed with no alert
choices.why: 5.1.2(i) requires explicit permission through the framework.

choices.text: App Store Connect sends a reminder email to the developer
choices.why: That email is for required-reason APIs missing from the manifest.

prompt: The planner adds an analytics SDK for one chart. What should you read before shipping it?
hint: The app answers for what its SDKs do.

choices.text: Only its licence, since privacy is the SDK maker's job
choices.why: The app is answerable for an SDK that tracks on its behalf.

choices.text: The SDK's own privacy manifest
choices.why: Right: it says what the SDK collects and whether it tracks, and Xcode combines it with yours.

choices.text: Its source code, line by line, for network calls
choices.why: Possible, but the manifest is where the SDK declares this, and it is short.

choices.text: Nothing: SDKs from Swift Package Manager are reviewed by Apple
choices.why: Apple does not review packages; you add them yourself.

prompt: What does the privacy manifest record that `Info.plist`'s usage strings do not?
hint: One says why the app asks; the other, what it does without asking.

choices.text: The sentence shown in the permission alert
choices.why: That is the usage string, in `Info.plist`.

choices.text: Data collected and required-reason APIs used
choices.why: Right, both quoted from Apple's page in section 06.

choices.text: The app's bundle identifier and its version
choices.why: Those are `Info.plist` keys from lesson 1.

choices.text: The certificate the app is signed with
choices.why: Signing is lesson 21 and has nothing to do with this file.

prompt: The planner keeps the last open course in `UserDefaults`, read only by itself. The reason code it declares is ___.
hint: Four characters, a period and a digit.

prompt: Run on `Lesson1.plist`, `check-privacy.swift` printed `1 missing`. What exit status did `echo $?` print?
hint: The last line of `check-privacy.swift`.

prompt: Adding `tracking` to the checker's words gave two `MISSING` lines. Why two?
hint: Tracking touches both files.

choices.text: The checker counts every word twice by mistake
choices.why: `camera` and `userdefaults` were each reported once in the same run.

choices.text: No usage string, and a manifest that says it does not track
choices.why: Right: tracking needs both its string and a manifest that admits it.

choices.text: `NSPrivacyTracking` has to list the advertising domains first
choices.why: Domains go in `NSPrivacyTrackingDomains`, which this checker does not read.

choices.text: A tracking app needs two reason codes for `UserDefaults`
choices.why: The `UserDefaults` line was `ok` in that run.

prompt: After a person denies the camera, what does the planner's button become?
hint: Guideline 5.1.1(iv): respect the setting, offer an alternative.

choices.text: An alert on launch until the camera is allowed
choices.why: That is pressure, which 5.1.1(iv) forbids, and it blocks the rest of the app.

choices.text: Nothing: the button is hidden, since a session needs no photo anyway
choices.why: Hiding it leaves the person no way to know why or to change it.

choices.text: A sentence that it is off, with a way to Settings
choices.why: Right, in the place where the camera would have been.

choices.text: The same button, which calls `requestAccess` again
choices.why: The call returns the stored no; the person would tap and see nothing.

prompt: `button(for:)` has no `default` case. What does that buy?
hint: What happens when a fifth state is added to `CameraAccess`?

choices.text: Faster code, since the compiler skips a branch
choices.why: Speed is not the point; checking is.

choices.text: A new state will not compile until it is given an answer
choices.why: Right: the compiler checks every case is handled.

choices.text: Nothing; Swift adds an empty default
choices.why: Swift adds no default; an unhandled case is a compile error.

choices.text: It lets `denied.swift` run without Foundation
choices.why: The file needs no Foundation anyway; that is not what `default` decides.

prompt: Put a camera permission's life in order, for a person who first says no and later changes their mind.
hint: Section 07's figure.
items: The person turns the switch on: `.authorized`

prompt: Which of these need a key or an entry in the planner's two privacy files? Choose all that apply.
hint: Usage strings for what asks; the manifest for required-reason APIs.

choices.text: Taking a photo with the camera
choices.why: Yes: `NSCameraUsageDescription`.

choices.text: Choosing a photo with `PhotosPicker`
choices.why: No: the picker runs outside the app.

choices.text: Keeping the last course in `UserDefaults`
choices.why: Yes: a required-reason API, `CA92.1`.

choices.text: Scheduling a reminder at a time the person set
choices.why: No: notifications ask with their own call and need neither file.

prompt: When should the planner call `requestAccess` for the camera?
hint: Asked out of context, people say no.

choices.text: At launch, so that every permission is settled at once
choices.why: Out of context, and the no it invites is permanent.

choices.text: During onboarding, on a screen explaining every feature
choices.why: Still before the person wants a photo; the moment of use is later.

choices.text: When the person taps the button that takes the photo
choices.why: Right: the request is in context and the reason is obvious.

choices.text: After a week, once the person trusts the app
choices.why: Timing by calendar is still out of context.
